title: Mardana and the rebab
hook: a Muslim musician, Bhai Mardana, becomes his lifelong companion; Mardana plays and Nanak sings

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying with the qazi, and a mind that had wandered home to a young horse. Your line was where is your mind right now. Where was yours, the last time you tried to give something your whole attention? Day thirty-one.

Think of the best duos you know. Two friends who finish each other's jokes. A singer and the guitarist who has played behind her for thirty years. One of them is the name on the poster, and the other one is the reason the song works. Guru Nanak had one of those. His name was Mardana. He came from Nanak's own village, Talwandi, and tradition says he was about ten years older. He was a Muslim, from a family of hereditary musicians, the kind of family that played at weddings and sang the genealogies of the village. And he carried an instrument everywhere he went. When Nanak came out of the river with something to say, Mardana is the one who gave it a tune. Today, the instrument.
screen: `EVERY GREAT SONG HAS TWO PEOPLE.` → `A MUSLIM MUSICIAN FROM TALWANDI.` → `HE CARRIED AN INSTRUMENT.`

segments.voice: The instrument was a rebab: a plucked string instrument with a wooden body, skin stretched across the front, and a deep, woody voice. It's the ancestor, or at least a cousin, of instruments played across Central and South Asia today. Picture how the two of them worked. Nanak would feel a hymn coming. Tradition says he would turn to his friend and say something like: Mardana, play the rebab, the Word is coming. And Mardana would find the note, and Nanak would sing. So from the very beginning, Sikh scripture wasn't something written down and read silently. It was sung. It was born as music. That's why the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga, by musical mode, and why, in a gurdwara today, the hymns are still sung to instruments. Now notice who is holding that rebab. A Muslim musician sat at the side of a teacher born into a Hindu family, and for decades they walked together, ate together and slept on the same roads. Remember the line from a few days ago: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Mardana is that line with a face and a pair of hands. Sikhs still honor him by name. A few verses in the scripture carry his name, and his descendants, called rababis, sang the hymns in Sikh gatherings for generations. And there's one more thing in the pairing worth keeping. Neither of them did it alone. The words needed the music, and the music needed the words. With this, the early years close: the boy at Talwandi, the river, the storehouse, the first words after. Tomorrow the two of them walk out of town.
screen: `THE REBAB — STRINGS, SKIN, WOOD.` · `MARDANA, PLAY. THE WORD IS COMING.` · `SCRIPTURE BORN AS MUSIC.` · `A MUSLIM MUSICIAN AT NANAK'S SIDE.` · then, large: `ONE PLAYS, ONE SINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one piece of music, all the way through. Any music. Pick something now, or let the bell's two minutes be the music. Don't do anything else while it plays. Don't check the time. When the song gets to the part you usually skip, stay. Notice the instrument underneath the voice, the one you normally don't hear. Somebody is playing it, so the singer can sing. The bell holds the time.
Rebab. The stringed instrument Bhai Mardana played beside Guru Nanak, so the hymns could be sung. Today's word.
Your line: one plays, one sings. Today, notice someone who makes your work possible from the side of the stage, and tell them so. Day thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sikh hymns are sung, not only read: in gurdwaras, musicians called ragis sing the scripture to instruments in the ragas it is arranged by, and Bhai Mardana is remembered as the first musician of the Sikh tradition.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the rebab, the string instrument of Bhai Mardana; the word came into Punjabi from Persian and Arabic.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old instrument in a museum.
what it means: the rebab Mardana played so Nanak could sing, which made Sikh scripture music from the start.
what a scholar hears: a Muslim hereditary musician at the founder's side for decades, and his descendants, the rababis, singing in the Sikh court for generations.

sources.ref: Bhai Gurdas, Var 1 (Mardana with the Guru on his travels)

notes: Mardana's age (about ten years older than Nanak) and his family as Mirasi hereditary musicians follow common tradition; confirm.
The saying 'Mardana, play the rebab, the Word is coming' is a janamsakhi motif, paraphrased; confirm the framing.

Saloks headed 'Mardana 1' in Bihagare ki Var (around Ang 553): whether they are addressed to Mardana or composed in his name is read differently; voice now says only that a few verses carry his name. Confirm Ang and framing.
Rababis (Mardana's descendants) as kirtan singers until the twentieth century; confirm.
Rebab described as the ancestor or cousin of instruments across Central and South Asia; kept deliberately loose. Confirm.
